newsitem.title: UK: World Bank watches for opportunities in euros.
newsitem.headline: World Bank watches for opportunities in euros.

text.p: The World Bank said on Wednesday it is looking at opportunities for raising money that could be denominated in the new euro currency, but that it was not seen as cost-effective at present.

A senior official of the World Bank, which is one of the top borrowers in international capital markets, told Reuters it was waiting for an opportunity to launch a bond which can be redenominated in euro.
"If it was cost-effective, we'd launch it (a euro Eurobond) tomorrow," senior manager of capital markets operations at the World Bank treasury Gumersindo Oliveros said.
The World Bank is widely regarded as an adventurous issuer which taps a broad spectrum of currencies. It launched the first-ever global bond in 1989.
The key innovation in the international bond markets this year has been the launch of Eurobonds which, when the euro is introduced, can be redenominated in that currency.
Under plans for European economic and monetary union (EMU), the single currency is due to be introduced on January 1, 1999.
Thus far, a handful of supranational groups and European borrowers have issued such bonds.

One syndicate manager at a German bank said he felt the reason the World Bank had not yet launched a euro Eurobond was that it did not have a vested interest in the EMU process, unlike, say. the European Investment Bank (EBRD) and the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development.
Both of those organisations have launched euro-Eurobonds.
"They have a vested interest in sponsoring the process but the World Bank does not have a political axe to grind," he said.
Euro Eurobonds are driven by concerns that deals in currencies which join the single European currency could become illiquid after EMU if the deals do not include this clause.
Under EMU, the euro is expected to run parallel with member states' national currencies until 2002.

J.P. Morgan pioneered the first such transaction for Austria in January which included a clause allowing future deals to be redenominated in the euro. Austria issued a bond in French francs which had an option to redenominate in euros if and when France adopted the currency.
Hot on its heels was a deal by the EIB, which has since done more such transactions.
Caisse Centrale du Credit Immobilier de France, Baden Wuerttemberg L-Finance NV, ABN AMRO Bank, Siemens, Societe Generale and the EBRD complete the list of euro-Eurobond issuers.
Despite some uncertainty in markets as to the EMU timetable, Oliveros said the World Bank was preparing itself for the advent of EMU and was closely monitoring developments.

"We look for cost-effective funding and up to now the benchmark issue in euros, or in currencies that can be redenominated into euros, have really not been cost-effective for us relative to arbitrage opportunities in other markets," Oliveros said. He was in London for a bond conference.
The World Bank plans to borrow up to $5.5 billion on the international capital markets between now and the end of its fiscal year in June, Oliverso added.
"Our fiscal year runs from July 1996 to June 1997 and we want to raise $13 billion to $14 billion equivalent on the international capital markets," he said.
"So far $8.5 billion equivalent has been raised. If we continue to have good market opportunities, like we have had so far, we will go up to $14 billion," he said.
He was referring to medium- and long-term borrowing.
In the 1996 calender year, the World Bank raised $13 billion and Oliveros said this amount could be matched in 1997.
"Beyond that our borrowing programme will depend of the level of disbursements we have on our loan portfolio and also the redemptions that are falling due," he said.
